_comment: Polynesian expansion batch 171 - Turner, Samoa A Hundred Years Ago (Gutenberg #14224), ch. 4-5 deity entries (Pava, Pili ma le Maa, the Stones, Le Sa, Salevao) and ch. 19. Topics 2 deity narratives, 5 ritual origin, 11 taboo. All passages are labeled paraphrase.

title.en: Pava Fled from the Eye of Tangaloa
title.zh: 帕瓦逃避坦加羅亞之眼

source.work: George Turner, Samoa A Hundred Years Ago and Long Before, ch. 4 (London 1884)

summary.en: Tangaloa, seeing the smoke of the children's fire, comes down from the heavens to Pava's house; a bowl of ava is upset by a creeping child, and in rage Tangaloa beats the child to death - then makes it live again. Pava in anger plucks a taro leaf, steps on it and goes off to Fiji, returning with the son of the king of Fiji; his emblem is the taro leaf, his people wear taro-leaf caps in battle, and he is seen in the rainbow. Another version has Pava fleeing from island to island, still pursued by the piercing eye of Tangaloa, until he reaches the district where the dreaded eye is no longer visible.
summary.zh: 坦加羅亞見孩童炊煙，自天而降至帕瓦家；孩童爬行間傾翻卡瓦碗，神怒而擊斃孩童——復又使之還生。帕瓦憤而摘芋葉踏之上天，往斐濟，後攜斐濟王子歸來；其神徽即芋葉，戰時其部眾皆戴芋葉之冠，彩虹即其所現。另一說謂帕瓦自一村一島輾轉逃避，坦加羅亞的利眼卻處處相隨，直至他抵達那無法再見神眼之地才得安居。

sensitivity.note: Deity legend; child-killing and revival recorded as in the tradition.

passages.text: This was the name of a war god on the south side of Upolu; it was originally the name of a man who came from the east end of the group. He and his wife went to work as usual in the bush and left their children in the house; the children kindled a fire to cook some food. Tangaloa, seeing the smoke, came down from the heavens; he found only the children, and inquired where their parents were - 'Gone to work', said they. 'Go and tell them I am here.' The children ran off and told them there was a chief in the house. Pava made haste home, found Tangaloa, and prepared a bowl of ava for him. A little child in creeping about the floor upset the ava; Tangaloa flew into a rage and beat the child to death; he again made it live, however, but Pava got up in anger, went out, plucked a taro leaf, stepped on to it and went off to Fiji. After a time he came back with a son of the king of Fiji, to the amazement of everybody, and when he died had a place in the Samoan pantheon.
passages.note: Paraphrase of George Turner, Samoa A Hundred Years Ago and Long Before, ch. 4 (1884); not verbatim.

passages.text: His emblem was a taro leaf, and all his adherents in going to battle were known by taro leaf caps; the slain of that particular village were also known by the round leaf cap. Pava was seen in the rainbow: if it was clear and reflected down on the village, that was a good omen; but if it appeared far inland, the sign was bad, and a veto on any fighting for that day at least. Another story places the killing of the child in the east end of the group, and says that Pava fled from place to place, and from island to island, to get away from the presence of Tangaloa; as soon, however, as he reached a fresh place and thought of remaining there, he saw the terrible eye of Tangaloa looking down on him. Off he went to another village or another island, but still the piercing eye of Tangaloa followed him, until he reached the district to which I have referred, and where the dreaded eye was no longer visible.
passages.note: Paraphrase of George Turner, Samoa A Hundred Years Ago and Long Before, ch. 4 (1884); not verbatim.

title.en: The Lizard and the Stone: Twin Gods of War Omens

region.zh: 烏波盧戰村（象徵性定位）

source.work: George Turner, Samoa A Hundred Years Ago and Long Before, ch. 4 (London 1884)

summary.en: Pili ma le Maa, twin gods worshipped in war, famine and pestilence: a lizard darting across the road means turn back at once; running ahead means go on to meet the enemy. Cocoa-nut leaves are plaited over the middle post of the great house, and the chiefs watch - the lizard coming straight down the matting is good, zigzag is bad; the priest sprinkles each man with cocoa-nut juice, saying 'May the road I take flow with blood'. Smooth stones of the stream stand in a temple, one making yams and fruit, the other sending fish to the nets.
summary.zh: 『蜥蜴與石』——戰、饑、疫之時共祀的雙神。蜥蜴橫穿道路則立即回返；奔跑向前則可迎敵。眾酋以椰葉編席裹住大屋中柱守候觀察：蜥蜴直落席上為吉，曲折而下為凶；臨行祭司以椰汁灑身並誦『願我所行之路血流成河』。溪中光石奉於廟中——一石司薯芋果實，一石司漁網之魚。

passages.text: Pili ma le Maa were the names of twin gods, and worshipped at certain villages in time of war, famine, and pestilence. The month of May was a specially fixed time for prayers and food offerings. The lizard was the guiding incarnation, and carefully watched in times of war: if in going to battle a lizard was seen darting across the road they returned at once; if it ran ahead, however, they were cheered and went right on to meet the enemy. Another plan in searching for an omen was to plait cocoa-nut leaves and cover the middle post of the great house, from the floor to the ridge pole, and there the chiefs sat and watched: if a lizard from the roof came straight down on the matting that was a good sign, but if it came down zigzag the omen was bad, and fighting suspended. Before going to the fight they met and were sprinkled with cocoa-nut juice by the priest, each at the same time uttering the prayer, 'May the road I take flow with blood.'
passages.note: Paraphrase of George Turner, Samoa A Hundred Years Ago and Long Before, ch. 4 (1884); not verbatim.

passages.text: Two unchiselled smooth stones of the stream were kept in a temple at one of the villages and guarded with great care; no stranger or over-curious person was allowed to go near the place, under penalty of a beating from the custodians of these gods. They represented good and not malicious death-causing gods: the one made the yams, bread, fruit and cocoa-nuts, and the other sent fish to the nets. Another stone was carefully housed in another village as the representative of a rain-making god: when there was over-much rain the stone was laid by the fire and kept heated till fine weather set in; in a time of drought the priest and his followers dressed up in fine mats and went in procession to the stream, dipped the stone and prayed for rain.
passages.note: Paraphrase of George Turner, Samoa A Hundred Years Ago and Long Before, ch. 4 (1884); not verbatim.

title.en: The Petrified Coward and the Settling Stones

region.en: Road to the plantations, Samoa (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 薩摩亞墾道旁（象徵性定位）

source.work: George Turner, Samoa A Hundred Years Ago and Long Before, ch. 4 (London 1884)

summary.en: A stone in the road was said to have been a petrified coward: he and his brother covenanted to be brave in battle, praying that whichever fled should be changed into a stone; one turned before the enemy and was so changed by the god Fe'e - and every worker passing to the plantations kissed, or rather smelled, the stone, death being the penalty for neglect. Two boundary stones were two young men who killed each other in a quarrel - 'Go and settle it at the stones' being the standing order of two villages noted for peace and order.
summary.zh: 道旁之石乃化形的懦夫：兄弟倆立誓臨陣不退，並求神立約——臨陣脫逃者當化為石。戰日一到，其一轉身而逃，遂被神費埃當場石化；農人往來墾地皆親吻——毋寧說『嗅』——此石，怠慢者將遭橫死。村界處另立雙石，乃兩個相殺而亡的青年——『到石前解決去』成了兩村永享太平的口諭。

passages.text: In a road leading to village plantations a stone stood which was said to have been a petrified coward. He and his brother entered into compact that they would be brave in battle, and implored their god that if either fled that one should be changed into a stone. The day came, the battle was fought, but one of the brothers turned and fled before the face of the enemy, and so was changed into a stone there and then by the god Fe'e. All the people as they passed inland to work in their plantations kissed, or rather smelled, the stone, and in coming back did the same; death was supposed to be the consequence of the neglect of this mark of deference to the power of the Fe'e.
passages.note: Paraphrase of George Turner, Samoa A Hundred Years Ago and Long Before, ch. 4 (1884); not verbatim.

passages.text: At the boundary line between two villages there were two stones, said to have been two young men who quarrelled, fought, and killed each other on that very spot, and whose bodies were immediately changed into stones. If any quarrel took place in either of these two villages there was never any general disturbance: 'Go and settle it at the stones' was the standing order; and so all who were inclined to be demonstrative in any affair of honesty or honour went to the stones and fought it out. If either of the duellists was knocked down that was the final settlement; no one else interfered, and so, by common consent in such matters, these two villages were noted for peace and order.
passages.note: Paraphrase of George Turner, Samoa A Hundred Years Ago and Long Before, ch. 4 (1884); not verbatim.

title.en: Salevao Becomes the Moon to Save Nonu

region.en: Court of the King of Tonga (symbolic pin)

source.work: George Turner, Samoa A Hundred Years Ago and Long Before, ch. 4 (London 1884)

summary.en: Visiting the king of Tonga, the worshipper Nonu disputes with him over the age of the moon and stakes his life on his belief that the moon is visible in the morning. Salevao, his god, appears in the night: 'Nonu, you are wrong; the moon is not now seen in the morning. But, lest you should be killed, I will go and be the moon in the horizon to-morrow morning, and make the king believe you were right after all.' In the morning Salevao, as the moon, was seen, and Nonu was saved - adding alike to reverence for the god and to the treasury of the priest.
summary.zh: 諾努訪湯加王，因月亮晨間是否可見一事與王爭執，竟以性命作注。守護神薩萊瓦奧夜間顯現：『諾努，你錯了；晨間本無月。但為免你被殺，明日清晨我將化身為月掛在地平線，使王信你原是對的。』翌晨薩萊瓦奧果然以月形現身，諾努得救——神之靈驗與祭司之庫房因此兩皆增光。

passages.text: Salevao was a war god in a number of villages, and incarnate in a dog - a white one usually: when he wagged his tail, barked, and dashed ahead in sight of the troops of the enemy it was a good sign, but to retreat or howl was a bad omen. A story of his kindness to Nonu, one of his worshippers, relates that when Nonu was on a visit to the King of Tonga he and the king had a dispute about the age of the moon: Nonu maintained that it was then to be seen in the morning; the king held that it was not visible in the morning. Nonu said he would stake his life on it; and so it was left for the morning to decide. In the night Salevao appeared to Nonu and said to him: 'Nonu, you are wrong; the moon is not now seen in the morning. But, lest you should be killed, I will go and be the moon in the horizon to-morrow morning, and make the king believe you were right after all, and so save your life.' In the morning Salevao, as the moon, was seen, and Nonu was saved - such stories added alike to reverence for the god and to the treasury of the priest.
passages.note: Paraphrase of George Turner, Samoa A Hundred Years Ago and Long Before, ch. 4 (1884); not verbatim.

title.en: Le Sa Sends the Caterpillars to Forage

region.zh: 烏波盧墾地（象徵性定位）

source.work: George Turner, Samoa A Hundred Years Ago and Long Before, ch. 4 (London 1884)

summary.en: In some places Le Sa was incarnate in an owl, more of an agricultural god who sent rain and abundance of food and was worshipped about April. He was prayed to and propitiated with offerings for the removal of caterpillars from the plantations, as they were thought to be servants under his orders to forage and punish; he was supposed to be fond of the bodies of thieves, and to go at once and devour them if prayed to do so. Bad-tempered parents frightened the children by saying they would call Le Sa to drink them up.
summary.zh: 萊薩或化身為鴞，主司農事賜雨豐穫，四月受祀；毛蟲侵田被視為神所遣之僕，藉以覓食懲罰，故須以祭品求其撤回。神尤喜食竊賊之身，一經祈求即往吞之；暴怒的父母以『叫萊薩來喝掉你』嚇唬孩童。

passages.text: In some places Le Sa was incarnate in an owl, was more of an agricultural god, who sent rain and abundance of food, and was worshipped about the month of April. He was prayed to and propitiated with offerings for the removal of caterpillars from the plantations, as they were thought to be servants under his orders to forage and punish. He was supposed to be fond of the bodies of thieves, and to go at once and devour them if prayed to do so; bad-tempered parents frightened the children by saying that they would call Le Sa to drink them up. In cases of sickness the patient went and weeded some piece of bush land as an offering to Le Sa; and the consequence was often a wonderful cure to the indolent dyspeptic!
passages.note: Paraphrase of George Turner, Samoa A Hundred Years Ago and Long Before, ch. 4 (1884); not verbatim.

passages.text: Le Sa in one place was a household god, and incarnate in the centipede: if any one was bitten by the reptile or otherwise ailing, an offering of a fine mat and a fan was presented, and the god entreated in some such words as: 'Lord! if you are angry, tell us the reason and send recovery.'
passages.note: Paraphrase of George Turner, Samoa A Hundred Years Ago and Long Before, ch. 4 (1884); not verbatim.
